# Why build an interactive chart?

An interactive chart lets the reader do things a static chart can't: **hover**
for exact values, **filter** to the part they care about, **zoom** into a crowded
region, **play** through time. That power has a price.

| The reader can... | The cost |
|-------------------|----------|
| Hover for exact values | Doesn't work on paper or in a PDF |
| Filter and zoom | Hard to share (e.g., social media) |
| Play through time | More to build, and more to *check* |
| Step through a story | Hides information behind a mouse |

## Two ways to get there

| | Packages | D3 + Claude |
|-|----------|-------------|
| Tools | `plotly`, `reactable` | D3.js, prompted |
| Code | Short R you could write | JavaScript you don't write |
| Limits | Only what the package does | Anything you can describe |

# Packages that wrap JavaScript

## `ggplotly()`: any ggplot, now interactive

```r
library(plotly)

plot <- gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp,
             size = pop, color = continent,
             label = country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10()

ggplotly(plot, tooltip = c("country", "pop"))
```

`ggplotly()` is a **translation**, and translations lose things. Tooltips show
raw aesthetic names (`x`, `colour`) and unrounded numbers; subtitles, captions,
and annotations can move or vanish; fonts and legends don't always survive.
When it gets messy, use [plotly directly](https://plotly.com/r/).

## `reactable()`: interactive tables

```r
library(reactable)

gapminder %>%
  reactable(
    searchable = TRUE, filterable = TRUE,
    highlight = TRUE, defaultPageSize = 5
  )
```

## Save it, then embed it

```r
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(
  ggplotly(plot),
  file = file.path('figs', 'gapminder.html'))
```

Then put it in a `.qmd` with an iframe, the same way you'll embed a D3 chart.

# Custom charts: D3 + Claude

[D3.js](https://d3js.org/) is the JavaScript library behind most custom
interactive graphics (The Pudding, NYT, The Guardian). It can build a custom
scale, a bespoke animation, linked views, or a layout no package offers. The
price is code: dozens of lines for what `geom_point()` does in one.

**You don't write D3. You prompt, and iterate.** You decide what the chart
should show, describe it precisely, and check that it's right. Claude writes the
JavaScript and revises until it looks right.

```{=typst}
#keypoint[
  *Verify against the data, not the code.* You can't check D3 by reading it, so
  build a static chart first and check it carefully. That static chart is your
  reference: the interactive version has to show the same numbers.
]
```

## The workflow

1. **Make a static chart** and verify it
2. **Sketch** what the interactive version should do: what moves, what hovers, what filters
3. **Prompt** Claude with your code, your data, and your sketch
4. **Iterate** until it looks right
5. **Verify** against the static chart and the data

## A prompt that works

```{=typst}
#block(width: 100%, inset: (left: 6pt, y: 2pt), stroke: (left: 1.5pt + hairline))[
  #text(fill: muted)[Here is my static chart (code below) and my data. Build an
  animated, interactive version in D3: \[describe your interaction\]. Add a
  tooltip, labeled axes, and a title that states the main takeaway. Put it in a
  single self-contained file called `d3-chart.html`, loading D3 from a CDN.
  Embed the data directly in the file.]
]
```

## Example: checking the gapminder bubble chart

The static 2007 chart says there are 142 countries, China and India are the
biggest bubbles, and life expectancy runs from about 40 to 83 years. So in the
D3 version:

1. Set the slider to **2007**: does it match the static chart?
2. **Hover** over China: do the values match the data?
3. **Count** the bubbles: 142?
4. Click **everything**: first and last year, each filter

```r
gapminder %>%
  filter(country == "China", year == 2007)

gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007) %>%
  nrow()
```

## Checks for any chart you didn't write

| Check | Ask |
|-----------|-----------------------------|
| The numbers | Hover several points: do they match the data? |
| The axes | Labels, units, ranges? Still works when resized? |
| The claim | Does the data support exactly what the title says? |
| The interaction | Does every control work, at the first and last year? |

If something is off, tell Claude exactly what's wrong and give it the right
value from your data.

## Gotchas

| Gotcha | Why |
|--------------|---------------------------|
| Embed the data | Browsers block a local `.html` from reading a local CSV, so the chart is blank |
| Load D3 from a CDN | The file links to a hosted copy of D3, so it needs internet |
| Check the console | Right-click → Inspect → Console shows red errors |
| Same folder, committed | The iframe can only find a file that's next to the `.qmd` |

```html
<iframe src="d3-chart.html" width="100%"
  height="500" style="border:none;"></iframe>
```

# Shiny apps

A Shiny app is a web page (the **UI**) connected to a computer running a live R
session (the **server**). It all lives in one file, `app.R`. Type `shiny` in
Positron and the snippet fills in the skeleton:

```r
library(shiny)
ui <- fluidPage()
server <- function(input, output, session) {}
shinyApp(ui, server)
```

Run it with the **Run App** button, or `shiny::runApp()` with the path to the
app file.

## Building one

| In the `ui` | In the `server` |
|-------------|-----------------|
| 1. Pick a layout function | 1. Make outputs with `render*()` |
| 2. Add input widgets | 2. Link outputs with `output$<id>` |
| 3. Add `*Output()` functions | 3. Link inputs with `input$<id>` |

## Layouts

Layout functions nest like Matryoshka dolls, so watch your parentheses and
commas.

| Layout | What it makes |
|--------|---------------|
| `fluidPage()` | The usual top level |
| `sidebarLayout()` | `sidebarPanel()` beside a `mainPanel()` |
| `navbarPage()` | A page of tabs, one `tabPanel()` each |
| `navbarMenu()` | A dropdown of tabs inside a navbar |

## Inputs collect, outputs display

| Input widget | Collects |
|--------------|----------|
| `sliderInput()` | A number from a range |
| `radioButtons()` | One choice from a list |
| `selectInput()` | A choice from a dropdown |
| `textInput()` | Free text |

| In the `ui` | In the `server` |
|-------------|-----------------|
| `plotOutput()` | `renderPlot()` |
| `textOutput()` | `renderText()` |
| `dataTableOutput()` | `renderDataTable()` |
| `imageOutput()` | `renderImage()` |

## Linking it together

The `inputId` in the UI becomes `input$xvar` in the server; the `outputId`
becomes `output$mpg_plot`.

```r
ui <- fluidPage(
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      radioButtons(
        inputId = "xvar",
        label = "Select the x-axis variable:",
        choices = c("hwy", "cty", "displ"))
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput(outputId = "mpg_plot")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$mpg_plot <- renderPlot({
    ggplot(mpg) +
      geom_point(aes_string(
        x = input$xvar, y = "hwy",
        color = "class"))
  })
}
```

## Common mistakes

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|--------------|-------------------------------|
| App won't start | Missing comma or parenthesis in the UI |
| Plot never appears | `outputId` doesn't match `output$<id>` |
| Input does nothing | Server never uses `input$<id>` |
| Output is blank | Code isn't inside a `render*()` |

## Deploy to Posit Connect Cloud (free)

Use **Posit Publisher**, built into Positron:

1. Click the **Posit Publisher** icon in the left sidebar
2. Under **Credentials**, click **+** → **Posit Connect Cloud** and sign in
3. Click **+** to add a deployment, pick `app.R`, check the project files, and
   click **Deploy Your Project**

## Extras

- **Themes:** add `theme = shinytheme("sandstone")` as the first argument of the
  top layout function (from the [shinythemes](https://rstudio.github.io/shinythemes/) package)
- **Fancier widgets:** the [shinyWidgets](https://dreamrs.github.io/shinyWidgets/) package
- **Reference:** the [cheatsheet](https://shiny.posit.co/r/articles/start/cheatsheet/) and [Mastering Shiny](https://mastering-shiny.org/)

# Choosing a tool

| You want... | Use |
|-------------------------------|----------------|
| Hover and zoom on a ggplot you have | `ggplotly()` |
| A searchable, sortable table | `reactable()` |
| A custom animation, scale, or layout | D3 + Claude |
| Readers to run R (filter, refit, recompute) | Shiny |

The first three save to plain `.html` files that work anywhere, including a
Quarto site on GitHub Pages. A Shiny app needs a live R session behind it, so it
has to be deployed to a server like Connect Cloud.
